Kernel Boundaries and Memory Protection
Protected OS model: applications request privileged services through system calls.
Application
User mode
System call
Controlled entry
Kernel service
Privileged mode
Address spaces and protection
Processes normally have separate address
spaces.
Threads share their process address space.
An MMU or MPU enforces access permissions
when configured.
Allocation and storage
A stack holds call frames and local state.
A heap supplies memory requested at run time.
Allocation reserves memory. Protection restricts
access.
Small RTOS deployments may use one shared address space without privilege separation.
9
Process
•A process is a running instance of a program.
•It has execution state and OS-managed resources.
•Processes can execute concurrently.
•They communicate through IPC mechanisms.
•A PCB records process-wide information.

Process Control Block
•The OS keeps process information in a Process Control Block (PCB).
•Per-thread control blocks store individual execution state.
11
Process Control Block
•Process ID and relationships
•Address-space information
•Open files and I/O resources
•Accounting and credentials
•References to thread state
•Exact fields depend on the OS
Thread
•A thread is an execution path within a process.
•Each thread has its own stack and CPU context.
•Threads share process memory and resources.
•The OS tracks per-thread state in a TCB.
•Shared access needs synchronization.
•Uncoordinated writes can cause data races.

Example: Display Process
Different Threads in Display Process
•Display time and date thread
•Display battery thread
•Display signal thread
•Display call thread
•Display message thread
•Display profile thread

Scheduling and Context Switching
Illustrative single-core trace: control task H has higher priority than logging task L.
CPU LHLH
0 1 3 5 6 ms
1 ms: H becomes ready and preempts L.
3 ms: H blocks for I/O; L resumes.
5 ms: I/O completes; H becomes ready.
Ready: eligible for CPU time.
Running: executing on the CPU.
Blocked: waiting for an event.
Context switch: save the current registers, program counter and stack pointer, then restore the next
task’s context.
Preemptive: the scheduler can interrupt execution. Cooperative: a task yields or blocks.
Concurrency overlaps progress; parallelism executes work simultaneously on multiple cores.

•The timing requirement determines which deadline misses are acceptable.
18

A miss violates the timing
specification.
Consequences depend on the
application.
Example: a control update with a
mandatory deadline.
Occasional deadline misses are
tolerable.
More or longer misses reduce service
quality.
Example: live audio or video
playback with occasional late
frames.

Timing Requirements and Response Time
Illustrative periodic control task: release at 0 ms, deadline at 10 ms, period 20 ms.
0
Release
2
Starts
5
Completes
10 ms
Deadline
Wait 2 ms Execute 3 ms Response time = 5 ms
Deadline margin = 5 ms
Release: when a job becomes eligible.
Execution time: CPU time used by the job.
Response time: release to completion.
Deadline: latest allowed completion.
Period: spacing between regular releases.
WCET: worst-case execution-time bound under
stated assumptions.
Jitter: variation in release or response timing.
A short execution time alone does not guarantee a deadline: waiting, interference and overhead also matter.

Real Time Operating System
•An RTOS supports applications with timing constraints.
•Its services aim for predictable response bounds.
•Footprint and supported hardware vary.
•Interrupt handling and scheduling affect response time.

Priority Inversion and Inheritance
Single core. H has high priority, M medium, and L low. H and L need the same mutex.
Step
Without inheritance
With priority inheritance
1. L owns the mutex
H requests it and blocks
H blocks. L inherits H’s priority.
2. M becomes ready
M preempts L; H keeps waiting
L runs ahead of M until it unlocks.
3. Mutex is released
H runs after L finally finishes
L finishes, unlocks; H can run
The inversion
H waits indirectly for M even though M does not
own the mutex.
The mitigation
Inheritance limits this interference. L returns to its
normal priority after release.
Keep critical sections short. Priority inheritance does not eliminate deadlock or all blocking.

Interrupt Handling and Deferred Work
Typical ISR model: acknowledge the event promptly, then let a task perform longer work.
Hardware event ISR starts Task becomes ready Task runs
Interrupt service routine (ISR)
Acknowledge the device and capture urgent state.
Signal deferred work through an ISR-safe
mechanism.
Avoid blocking operations.
Deferred task
Processes the data in normal task context.
Competes with other ready tasks.
Can use permitted blocking APIs.
Interrupt latency: interrupt assertion to ISR entry in this model.
Dispatch latency: time to start the selected task. End-to-end response also includes ISR work and
scheduling delays.
